title: Times Stories
child_idea: In a times story every group is the same size, so we draw equal boxes in a strip. We find the total, then do the next step. Twice as many means two equal strips.

topics: Equal-group word problems with products within 40 (Primary 1, Multiplication and Division 3.1 to 3.4, p. 31)
One extra step after a total: add or take away (Primary 1, Addition and Subtraction, p. 31)
Drawing a strip (bar model) and "twice as many" or "3 times as many" (not named in the Primary 1 syllabus topics)
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. Equal-group stories with totals within 40, and one extra step of adding or taking away, are in the school Primary 1 syllabus (p. 31); Start here stays there (totals to 20 for the groups, answers within 40). BEYOND PRIMARY 1 ON PURPOSE: drawing the story as a strip (a bar model: schools use it from Primary 2, and this program says strip to children and "strips (called bar models at school)" to parents) and "twice as many" and "3 times as many" comparisons, with a total or a transfer, at Think harder and Go further. Owner decision of 22 Oct 2026: strong content with scaffolding, said plainly to families on the parent page. The strip is the whole lesson: if a child cannot draw it, they may use cups of counters. Do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned or syllabus-aligned. Reading order (owner default): 3 groups of 5 is 3 × 5; either order is accepted. Contest tags (tutor only): twice as many is two equal strips, a transfer after twice as many (T4), a total with a hidden unit (G3), doubling again and again (Investigation).

contest_moves: twice as many is two equal strips, not 2 more (T2, T3)
a transfer after twice as many: Ali gives some so they have the same (T4)
a total with a hidden unit: 3 times as many, 24 together (G3)
objectives: Draw a story with same-size groups as a strip of equal boxes, write the number in each box and find the total.
Solve a story with a total and one more step: loose items added, or items taken away.
Match a story to its strip, and say when the boxes are not all the same.
Think harder: draw "twice as many" as two equal strips (not 2 more), find the total of two children, and use a transfer to make two amounts equal.
Go further: a story with groups of different sizes and a hidden start, and "3 times as many" with a total.

remember: Two strips and the gap: who has more, and how many more (earlier this term)
4 groups of 5 is 4 × 5: how many groups, how many in each, how many in all (earlier this term)
One step at a time: 6 and 4 more, then give away 3 (Term 1)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and adding small numbers. Nothing from an earlier lesson is needed: the warm-up shows two strips with a picture, shows 4 bags of 5 and shows a two-step story with its two steps written out. The words strip, box, each, loose and twice as many are taught in Explore and the Mini-lesson.
holiday_topics_revisited: Same-size groups as repeated adding (taught again, no holiday lesson needed)
joining_cold.note: Term 2 Lessons 2 and 5 to 8 build on each other and Term 2 Lesson 10 uses strips for price stories, so try not to miss this lesson. A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Term 2 Lesson 10. A child who joins here can follow, because the warm-up shows a strip, same-size groups and a two-step story with pictures; the Mini-lesson then draws the strip step by step.

child: The printed workbook, kept flat, with the strips page (page 6) cut into strips by a grown-up before the lesson (three of the strips cut after 6 cells)
About 20 small things of one kind (counters, buttons, dry pasta, coins). Not food
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: Two or three paper strips and some counters to show on camera if you wish
kit_pages: Strips page (page 6): ten strips of 10 equal cells in two colours, with dotted lines between the cells. Before the lesson a grown-up cuts the page into the ten strips (cut between the strips, not between the cells) and cuts three of them after 6 cells. Nobody cuts during the lesson
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. A grown-up does all the cutting before the lesson; children do not use scissors. If the strips are not cut, children use counters in rows (Explore round 4) or draw boxes in a row. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears. Nothing in Explore needs more than 20 counters, 3 cups and 3 pre-cut strips.

timing.notes: Opening is 2 minutes (the routine and rules were taught earlier in the term; give the recording, muting and camera notice after the greeting). Explore has 13 minutes of cups, counters and counters in rows: a story as a strip, matching strips to stories, a total plus loose items, and twice as many; the slides with a question show the question first and the strip comes on an answer slide. The mini-lesson has 12 because it draws the strip step by step, adds the two-step story and the twice-as-many strip. The workbook has 30 minutes: Start here is modelled at 8 and 9 minutes for pages 1 and 2 (17 minutes for a middle child), so about 3 minutes remain for choosing; Think harder is normally a home page for a middle child, and the guide says so. The last 4 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.
skip_order: Start with: cut the Mini-lesson check slide to two of the three stories
Then: shorten Explore round 2 (match the strip) to one story
Then: take the extra minutes from the flex time

sneak_peek.q1: Ali has 3 bags. Each bag has 4 sweets. How many sweets does Ali have in all? You may draw to help.
sneak_peek.q2: Mei has 5 stickers. Ben has twice as many stickers as Mei. How many stickers do they have together? Then write or draw how you know.
sneak_peek.a2: 15. Ben has twice as many as Mei: 5 and 5, which is 10. Mei has 5 and Ben has 10, so together they have 15.

opening.action: Gather your workbook, strips, pencil, paper, counters and cups. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Touch the numbers and say your answers before I say them. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Say each answer out loud before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Put counters in cups, lay out strips and test each story. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Put counters in cups, lay strips next to each story and make twice as many.

exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

slides.title: Times Stories

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Draw a story as strips, then solve it.

slides.note: Term 2 Lesson 8, 90 minutes. Objective: draw an equal-group story as a strip, solve a story with one more step, and draw twice as many as two equal strips. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 25, mini-lesson 25 to 37, brain break 37 to 41, workbook 41 to 71, talk 71 to 77, exit ticket 77 to 83, look-back 83 to 86, flex time and goodbye 86 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Say the recording notice in one line after the greeting: you and the screen only; a child may keep the camera off. Say plainly to grown-ups that equal-group stories are Primary 1 work and that drawing strips and twice as many go a little further.
slides.subtitle: Equal strips, one step at a time

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: two strips

blocks.text: A longer strip has more. The gap is how many more.

slides.note: This is the two-strips idea from earlier in the term, taught again from scratch: Ali has 9 and Mei has 5. The longer strip has more. The gap is the extra part, how many more. Ask: who has more (Ali), and how many more (4)? Children answer aloud or with fingers. A child who is unsure counts up from 5 to 9 on fingers. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Same-size groups

blocks.text: 4 groups of 5. Every bag has the same number.

items: How many groups?
How many in each?
How many in all?

slides.note: This is the equal-groups idea from earlier in the term, taught again from scratch: 4 bags with 5 pencils in each bag is 4 groups of 5, and there are 20 pencils in all. Ask the three questions on the slide: 4 groups, 5 in each, 20 in all. Children answer aloud or with fingers. A child who is unsure counts the pencils in one bag, then counts in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20.

slides.title: One step at a time

rows: Ali has 6 stickers and gets 4 more.

items: 6 and 4 more
then take away 3

slides.note: This is Term 1 again: one operation in each step. Step 1: 6 and 4 more is 10. Step 2: 10 take away 3 is 7. Ask for step 1 first (10), then step 2 (7). Children answer aloud or with fingers. A child who is unsure uses counters: 6 and 4 more, then push 3 away. Say: we do one step at a time, and we write each step.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Ali has 3 bags.
Each bag has 4 sweets.
How many sweets does Ali have in all?
You may draw to help.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Mei has 5 stickers.
Ben has twice as many stickers as Mei.
How many stickers do they have together?
Then write or draw how you know.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag; 12 sweets) is an access question: any child can draw it or count it out; the empty bags are there to draw in. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: twice as many as 5 is 10, and 5 and 10 together are 15. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Answers: 12; 15. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: cups and a strip

items: Put 3 cups on the table.
Put 5 counters in each cup.
Draw 3 boxes in a row. Write 5 in each box.
How many counters in all?

slides.note: Round 1, about 3 minutes. Objects first. Children put 5 counters in each of 3 cups, then draw one strip of 3 boxes on their own paper: each box is one cup. They write 5 in each box and find the total: 15 (count in fives). Say the words once: each cup is a box; every box is the same size, so it is a strip of equal boxes. The picture shows the strip; the question mark is the total. A child with fewer counters uses 2 cups of 4. If time allows, repeat with 4 cups of 3. Do not ask for a number sentence yet. The strip comes on the answer slide, after the children have built their own.

slides.title: Which strip is the story?

blocks.text: Ben has 4 bags. Each bag has 3 sweets. Show 1, 2 or 3 fingers.

slides.note: Round 2, about 4 minutes. Read the story: Ben has 4 bags with 3 sweets in each bag. Children show 1, 2 or 3 fingers for the strip that matches. Strip 1 is right: 4 boxes with 3 in each box. Strip 2 is 3 boxes of 4 (the numbers swapped). Strip 3 has 4 boxes but the last box is 2, so the boxes are not all the same. Do not name a child with a wrong answer. Then ask: what is the total (12)? Then give a second story with the same strips: Mei has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag (strip 2, 12).

slides.title: A total and some loose ones

items: Put 3 cups on the table with 5 counters in each cup.
Put 2 more counters on the table. They are loose: not in a cup.
How many counters are there in all?

slides.note: Round 3, about 3 minutes. Children keep the 3 cups of 5 and add 2 loose counters (loose means not in a cup). They count the cups first: 15, then the loose ones: 17. The strip shows 3 boxes of 5 and one smaller box of 2 in a different colour. Say: first the boxes, then the loose ones, one step at a time. Ask: what did we do first (3 groups of 5 is 15)? What next (15 and 2 more is 17)? A child who writes 5 + 3 + 2 has not drawn equal boxes: ask them to build it with cups.

slides.title: Twice as many

items: Make Mei a strip of 6: a row of 6 counters.
Ali has twice as many. Make Ali a strip the same as Mei’s, and then another the same.
How many counters has Ali? How many are there together?

slides.note: Round 4, about 3 minutes. Children make Mei a row of 6 counters (or use a pre-cut paper strip of 6 cells: a grown-up cut these before the lesson, nobody cuts during the lesson). Mei has 1 strip. Ali has twice as many: two rows the same as Mei’s, 6 and 6, which is 12. Together they have 18. Ask: is twice as many the same as 2 more? Mei has 6, and 2 more would be 8; twice as many is 12. Key idea: twice as many is two equal strips. A child who says 8 has added 2: put Ali’s two strips next to Mei’s one. The strips come on the answer slide, after the children have answered.

slides.title: Draw the story

items: Read it.
Draw equal boxes.
Write the number in each box.
Find the total.

blocks.text: 3 bags with 5 sweets in each bag.

slides.note: The four steps of a times story. Read it (3 bags with 5 sweets in each bag). Draw equal boxes: one box for each bag, 3 boxes. Write the number in each box: 5. Find the total: count in fives, 5, 10, 15; 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, or 3 × 5 = 15. Ask: how many boxes, what is in each box, what is the total? Say the unit once: every box is the same size. A child who draws 5 boxes with 3 in each has swapped the numbers: re-read the story. The strip comes on the answer slide, after the children have answered.

slides.title: A total, then one more step

blocks.text: 4 boxes of 5 pens and 6 loose pens.

slides.note: A second step. Ali has 4 boxes with 5 pens in each box, and 6 loose pens. Draw 4 equal boxes of 5 and one more box of 6 in a different colour. Step 1: the pens in boxes, 4 groups of 5 is 20. Step 2: add the loose pens, 20 + 6 = 26. Ask: which step comes first? What does the different colour show? The table has question marks: let children say each total before you say it. Say: one operation in each step (Term 1). If the loose pens were given away, we would take away in step 2.

slides.title: Twice as many

blocks.text: Mei has 8 stickers. Ali has twice as many.
Twice as many is two equal strips. It is not 2 more.

slides.note: Beyond Primary 1 on purpose. Mei has 8 stickers. Ali has twice as many: two strips the same as Mei’s, 8 and 8, which is 16. Together they have 8 and 16, which is 24. Ask: how many strips for Mei (1)? For Ali (2)? How many for both together (3 strips of 8)? Say it plainly: twice as many is two equal strips, not 2 more. Three times as many would be three equal strips (Go further). A child who says 10 has added 2: compare Ali’s strip with Mei’s. The strips and the table come on the answer slide, after the children have answered.

slides.title: Your turn

blocks.text: Draw a strip. Write each step. Say the total.

items: 3 bags of 4 sweets
5 boxes of 2 pens and 3 loose pens
Mei has 5. Ali has twice as many.

slides.note: Each child draws the three strips on their own paper and writes the answers. Walk the cameras; do not ask children to hold papers up. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Answers: 12 sweets; 5 boxes of 2 is 10, and 3 loose pens make 13 pens; Ali has 10 stickers and together they have 15. Children may use counters or cups.

slides.title: Check: draw the strip

rows: 5 boxes of 2 pens and 3 loose pens
Mei has 5. Ali has twice as many.

slides.note: Answers: 12 sweets; 13 pens (5 groups of 2 is 10, and 3 loose pens make 13); Ali has 10 stickers and together they have 15. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can tick their own work. Children tick their own with a tick. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Clap in groups

blocks.text: I say a story. Clap softly in groups and pause.
Say the total out loud together.
Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call: 3 groups of 2 (clap 2, pause, clap 2, pause, clap 2: 6), 4 groups of 3 (12), 2 groups of 5 (10), 3 groups of 4 (12). Then one twice as many: clap 4 for Mei, then twice as many for Ali (two claps of 4: 8). Children clap softly or tap their thighs, pausing between groups, and say the total together. No equipment, no running, a little clear space. A child may stay seated and tap the table.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder. Question 1: fill in the numbers in the strip for 3 bags of 5 sweets. Question 2: 4 boxes of 3 pencils, fill in the blanks. Question 3: choose the strip that matches the story (5 bags of 2 sweets).

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own page. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q1 5, 5, 5 in the boxes and 15 sweets; Q2 4 groups of 3 = 12 and 12 pencils (either order is right); Q3 strip 2.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 6. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 4 to 6 aloud. Question 4: 3 boxes of 5 pens and 2 loose pens. Question 5: draw a strip for 2 bags of 6 sweets. Question 6: 4 bags of 3 marbles and then some marbles lost.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q4 15 pens in the boxes and 17 pens in all; Q5 2 equal boxes of 6 and 12 sweets; Q6 12 marbles in the bags and 10 marbles now.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Different groups and 3 times as many
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. Not finished? Pages 3 to 5 are for home too.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: MEI HAS 8 STICKERS
items: Ali has twice as many as Mei.

blocks.text: Does twice as many mean 2 more? How could we be sure?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Children make Mei’s strip of 8 and Ali’s strip of twice as many with counters or paper strips, then try another number such as 5 or 6. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: no. Twice as many is two equal strips: 8 and 8 is 16, which is 8 more than Mei, not 2 more. Mei has 8, so 2 more would be 10. Repeat each child’s answer in your own words for the recording. Do not claim it is proved for every number: we tested a few and used the strips.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Together: 5 and 10 make 15.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone’s earlier answer. Mei has 5. Ben has twice as many: two strips of 5, which is 10. Together they have 5 and 10, which is 15. Puzzle 1: 3 bags of 4 sweets is 12 sweets.

slides.title: Exit ticket
slides.note: Children answer on page 5. Read E1, E2 and E3 aloud, including the four number sentences of E1 (the questions and the four options are on the slide). Children tick their own ticket against the next slide. Nobody holds paper to the camera and there is no private chat.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own ticket. Answers: option 2, 4 × 5; 13 marbles; 10 sweets.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide). You then help in the open session next lesson. Never a direct message to a child. The Next time I will try row is optional.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Picture Equations
Have ready: your Term 2 Lesson 9 workbook with its counters page (page 6) and its shape cards page (page 7) cut out by a grown-up, about 30 small counters, 2 cups, pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional slides and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: what if?

blocks.text: Dev has 3 times as many stickers as Siti. Who has more? How many more?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Siti has 6 stickers. Dev has 3 times as many: three strips of 6, which is 18. Dev has 18 and Siti has 6, so Dev has 12 more. Take two answers and move on. This repeats the twice-as-many idea with three strips.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Is twice as many ever the same as 2 more?
Draw a strip story. Ask your grown-up.
Show a toy 3 cups of 4 counters

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

lines.text: Greet the whole group warmly, before the recording starts. Check that you can see each child, or ask the grown-up.
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, and your strips, cups, counters and workbook on the table. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Start the recording now. Do not use children's first names on the recording.
@rec
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Today we draw stories as strips. Every box in the strip is the same size. Then we solve the story, one step at a time.

Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. Say the notice before you start the recording, and do not use children's first names once it is running. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced earlier in the term: do not re-teach them.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody holds paper to the camera. The first recording of the term shows the full routine.
@rec
Two strips. Ali has 9 and Mei has 5. The longer strip has more. The gap is how many more.
Who has more? How many more?
Check by counting up from five to nine on your fingers: six, seven, eight, nine. That is 4 jumps.
Same-size groups. 4 bags with 5 pencils in each bag. That is 4 groups of 5.
How many groups? How many in each group? How many pencils in all?
Count in fives to check: five, ten, fifteen, twenty.
One step at a time. Ali has 6 stickers and gets 4 more. That is step one. Then he gives away 3. That is step two.
Step one: 6 and 4 more. How many does Ali have?
Step two: take away 3. How many does he have now?
Children try one more with counters: Mei has 8 and gets 5 more, then gives away 6.
How many does Mei have at the end?
If a child is unsure about the strips, count up on fingers from 5 to 9. For the groups, count the pencils in one bag, then count in fives. For the steps, use counters: 6 and 4 more, then push 3 away.

Answers: Ali, 4 more; 4, 5, 20; 10, 7; 7. Children answer with a whisper, fingers or hands. Nobody writes. Do not say times as many yet. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and adding small numbers.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Ali has 3 bags. Each bag has 4 sweets. How many sweets does Ali have in all? You may draw to help.
Children draw or count and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Mei has 5 stickers. Ben has twice as many stickers as Mei. How many stickers do they have together? Then write or draw how you know.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.

Puzzle 1 answer: 12 sweets. Puzzle 2 answer: 15 (Ben has 10, and Mei has 5). Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew two groups of 5 for Ben, or who added 5 and 5 and then 5 more). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Your hands are the teachers. Put 3 cups on the table with 5 counters in each cup. Now draw 3 boxes in a row on your paper, one box for each cup. Write 5 in each box.
Children put 5 counters in each of 3 cups, then draw 3 boxes and write 5 in each.
How many counters are there in all? Count in fives.
Every box is the same size, so it is a strip of equal boxes. Each cup is a box.
Round two. Which strip is the story? Ben has 4 bags. Each bag has 3 sweets. Show one, two or three fingers.
Which strip? One, two or three fingers.
Strip one has 4 boxes with 3 in each box. Strip two has 3 boxes of 4. Strip three has 4 boxes, but the last box is 2, so the boxes are not equal.
How many sweets does Ben have in all?
Mei has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag. Which strip is Mei’s?
Round three. Keep 3 cups with 5 counters in each cup. Now put 2 more counters on the table. They are loose: not in a cup.
Children keep 3 cups of 5 and add 2 loose counters.
How many counters are there in the cups? Then how many in all?
First the boxes, then the loose ones. One step at a time. Now push 3 counters away.
How many counters are left on the table?
Round four. Make a row of 6 counters for Mei. Ali has twice as many. Make Ali a row the same as Mei’s, and then another row the same.
Children make Mei’s row of 6 counters and Ali’s two rows of 6 (counters in rows, or pre-cut paper strips of 6 cells; nobody uses scissors in the lesson).
How many cells has Ali? How many are there together?
Is twice as many the same as 2 more? Why not?
Twice as many is two equal strips.

A child who cannot draw boxes: use the cups of counters, or counters in rows. A child who says Ali has 8: put Ali’s two strips next to Mei’s one and count. A child who loses count in round 3: say the cups first (15), then the loose ones.

Main room only; children say their answers aloud and show fingers; you cannot see builds on small tiles. Answers: 15; 12; strip 1, 12 sweets, strip 2; 15 and 2 more is 17, then 14; Ali has 12, together 18, not 2 more (that would be 8). Nothing here needs more than 20 counters, 3 cups and 3 pre-cut strips. Nobody uses scissors in the lesson.
@rec
A times story in four steps. Read it. Draw equal boxes. Write the number in each box. Find the total. Three bags with 5 sweets in each bag.
How many boxes? What is in each box? What is the total?
3 boxes, 5 in each box: 15 in all.
Now a second step. Ali has 4 boxes with 5 pens in each box, and 6 loose pens. We draw 4 equal boxes, and then one more box in a different colour for the loose pens.
Which step comes first? What is step one, and what is the total?
Step two: add the loose pens. How many pens are there in all?
What if Ali gave away 6 pens instead of finding 6 more? Which step would change, and what is the answer?
Twice as many. Mei has 8 stickers. Ali has twice as many. Twice as many is two equal strips. It is not 2 more.
How many stickers does Ali have? How many do they have together?
We draw Ali’s strip two times as long: 8 and 8, which is 16. Together 8 and 16 make 24.
Three times as many would be three equal strips. We will try that on page 4.
Your turn. Draw a strip for each story and write the answer. 3 bags of 4 sweets. 5 boxes of 2 pens and 3 loose pens. Mei has 5. Ali has twice as many.
Children draw the strips and write the answers on their own paper.
Twelve sweets. Thirteen pens. Ali has ten, and together they have fifteen. Tick your own.

Equal-group stories are within the Primary 1 syllabus; drawing strips and twice as many go a little further, so keep the pace gentle and use the pictures. start.text: Mei has 3 bags. Each bag has 5 sweets. Write the number in each box of the strip. Then fill in the blank.
start.hint: Each box is one bag. Write the same number in every box. Then count in fives.
start.solution: There are 3 bags, so 3 boxes, and each box is 5 sweets. 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so Mei has 15 sweets in all.

start.text: Ben has 4 boxes. Each box has 3 pencils. How many pencils does Ben have in all?
start.answer: 4 groups of 3 = 12 (3 groups of 4 = 12 is also right); 12 pencils
start.hint: Write the number of boxes first. Then the number of pencils in each box.
start.solution: 4 boxes with 3 pencils in each box: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So 4 groups of 3 = 12 and Ben has 12 pencils. Either order gives the right total: if a child writes 3 groups of 4 = 12, ask 'how many boxes?'.
mistakes: Drawing 3 boxes with 4 in each box (the total is right, so ask 'how many boxes?').

start.text: Siti has 5 bags. Each bag has 2 sweets. Which strip shows Siti’s sweets? Write its number in the bracket.
start.hint: Look at the number of boxes and the number in each box. Are all the boxes the same?
start.solution: Strip 2 has 5 boxes with 2 in each box: 5 bags of 2 sweets. Strip 1 has 2 boxes of 5. Strip 3 has 5 boxes but the last box has 1, so the boxes are not equal.
mistakes: Choosing strip 1 because it has the same numbers.
Not noticing that the last box of strip 3 is smaller.

start.text: Ali has 3 boxes with 5 pens in each box. He also has 2 loose pens. How many pens does Ali have in all?
start.answer: 15 pens in the boxes; 17 pens in all
start.hint: Find the pens in the boxes first. Then add the loose pens.
start.solution: Step 1: 3 boxes of 5 pens is 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. Step 2: 15 and 2 loose pens make 17 pens in all.

start.text: Mei has 2 bags. Each bag has 6 sweets. Draw a strip. Then fill in the blank.
start.answer: A strip of 2 boxes with 6 in each box; 12 sweets
start.hint: Draw 2 boxes the same size in a row. Write 6 in each box.
start.solution: 2 bags with 6 sweets in each bag: draw 2 equal boxes and write 6 in each. 6 + 6 = 12, so Mei has 12 sweets in all.
mistakes: Drawing boxes that are not the same size.

start.text: Ravi has 4 bags with 3 marbles in each bag. He loses 2 marbles. How many marbles does Ravi have now?
start.answer: 12 marbles in the bags; 10 marbles now
start.hint: Find the marbles in the bags first. Then take away the marbles he loses.
start.solution: Step 1: 4 bags of 3 marbles is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Step 2: he loses 2, so 12 - 2 = 10 marbles are left.

think.text: Jenny has 3 boxes with 6 pens in each box and 5 loose pens. She gives 8 pens away.
think.hint: Do one step at a time: the boxes, then the loose pens, then the pens she gives away.
think.solution: Step 1: 3 boxes of 6 is 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Step 2: 18 and 5 loose pens make 23. Step 3: 23 take away 8 is 15 pens left.
mistakes: Taking away 8 from 18 before adding the loose pens.

think.text: Mei has 7 marbles. Ali has twice as many marbles as Mei.
think.hint: Draw Mei’s strip. Ali’s strip is two strips the same as Mei’s.
think.solution: Mei’s strip is 7. Ali has twice as many: 7 and 7, which is 14. Together they have 7 + 14 = 21 marbles.

think.text: Mei has 4 stickers. Ravi has twice as many stickers as Mei. Jenny says Ravi has 6 stickers.

parts.text: Is Jenny correct? Circle Yes or No.

think.hint: Twice as many is two strips the same as Mei’s. Draw them.
think.solution: Mei has 4, so Ravi has two strips of 4: 4 + 4 = 8 stickers. Jenny added 2 to 4 to get 6, but twice as many is not 2 more. So Jenny is not correct.

think.text: Ali has twice as many cards as Mei. Ali has 24 cards. Ali gives some cards to Mei. Then they have the same number of cards.
think.hint: Ali’s strip is two strips the same as Mei’s. Then share the gap into two equal parts.
think.solution: Ali has two strips of 12, so Mei has 12. The gap is 12. Ali gives half of the gap: two equal parts of 12 are 6 and 6, so he gives 6. Then Ali has 24 - 6 = 18 and Mei has 12 + 6 = 18. They have the same number.

go.text: Wei puts 3 stickers on each of 4 cards. He puts 2 stickers on each of 5 other cards. He also has 4 stickers in his hand.
go.hint: Find the stickers on each set of cards. Then add the stickers in his hand.
go.solution: 4 cards with 3 stickers: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. 5 cards with 2 stickers: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. 12 + 10 + 4 = 26 stickers at first (the 4 in his hand count too).
mistakes: Forgetting the 4 stickers in his hand.
Using 3 for both sets of cards.

go.text: Siti has 5 marbles. Ravi has 3 times as many marbles as Siti.
go.hint: Ravi’s strip is three strips the same as Siti’s.
go.solution: Siti’s strip is 5. Ravi has 3 times as many: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. Together: 5 + 15 = 20 marbles.

go.text: Kumar has 3 times as many pens as Lily. They have 24 pens together.
go.hint: Draw 1 box for Lily and 3 boxes for Kumar. How many equal boxes in all?
go.solution: Lily has 1 box and Kumar has 3 boxes, so there are 4 equal boxes. 24 pens in 4 equal boxes is 6 in each box (6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24). Lily has 6 and Kumar has 18. Check: 3 × 6 = 18 and 6 + 18 = 24.

investigation.title: Twice, and twice again
investigation.first: Mei has 3 stickers. Ali has twice as many. How many stickers does Ali have? Now Ben has twice as many as Ali.
investigation.text: Jenny has twice as many stickers as Ben. Write how many stickers Mei, Ali, Ben and Jenny each have. What do you notice?
investigation.answer: Mei 3, Ali 6, Ben 12, Jenny 24. Each child has twice as many as the child before, so each strip is twice as long as the one before. The numbers double each time: 3, 6, 12, 24.
investigation.look_for: A child who draws or builds each strip as two copies of the strip before, writes 3, 6, 12, 24 and notices that each number is double the last. Credit a child who says the strips get twice as long, or who checks 12 + 12. Do not mark down a child who finds only Ali and Ben.
mistakes: Writing twice as many as 3 for every child.

talk.question: Mei has 8 stickers. Ali has twice as many as Mei. Does twice as many mean 2 more? How could we be sure?
talk.answer: No. Twice as many is two equal strips: 8 and 8 is 16, which is 8 more than Mei, not 2 more (that would be 10). We test 8 and another number, and the strips show why. A few tests plus the picture are good evidence.
talk.look_for: A child who draws or builds Mei’s strip and Ali’s two strips, who tests another number, or who says twice is the number added to itself. Not just "yes" or "no".

exit.text: Ali has 4 bags. Each bag has 5 sweets. Which number sentence finds how many sweets Ali has in all? Write its number in the bracket.
exit.solution: 4 bags with 5 sweets in each bag is 4 groups of 5, which is 4 × 5. Adding 4 + 5 joins the numbers of bags and sweets. 5 - 4 finds a gap.

exit.text: Lily has 2 bags with 5 marbles in each bag. She also has 3 loose marbles. How many marbles does Lily have in all?
exit.solution: Step 1: 2 bags of 5 marbles is 10. Step 2: 10 and 3 loose marbles make 13 marbles in all.

exit.text: Ravi has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag. He eats 2 sweets. How many sweets does Ravi have now?
exit.solution: Step 1: 3 bags of 4 sweets is 12. Step 2: he eats 2, so 12 - 2 = 10 sweets are left.

home_practice.text: Siti has 4 bags. Each bag has 2 sweets. Fill in the blanks. [] × [] = [2]. Siti has [2] sweets in all.
home_practice.solution: 4 bags with 2 sweets in each bag: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.

home_practice.text: Ali has 3 boxes with 4 pens in each box and 5 loose pens. He has [2] pens in all.
home_practice.solution: 3 boxes of 4 pens is 12. 12 and 5 loose pens make 17.

home_practice.text: Mei has 4 bags with 4 stickers in each bag. She gives 3 stickers away. Mei has [2] stickers left.
home_practice.solution: 4 bags of 4 stickers is 16. 16 take away 3 is 13.

home_practice.text: Wei has 9 marbles. Ravi has twice as many marbles as Wei. They have [2] marbles together.
Mei has 4 stickers. Ali has 3 times as many stickers as Mei. Ben has 5 more stickers than Ali. Ben has [2] stickers.
home_practice.solution: Ali has 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 stickers. Ben has 12 + 5 = 17 stickers.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Is twice as many ever the same as 2 more? Try 2, then 3, then 8, with strips. Can you find a number where they are the same?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Make a strip for 2, then twice as many. Try 3 and 8 as well.
menu.answer: 2 makes 4 and 4 (the same); 3 makes 6 and 5; 8 makes 16 and 10. Only 2 works: twice as many is the number added to itself, so it equals 2 more only when the number is 2.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Draw a strip story with bags and sweets, or with twice as many. Write the number in each box. Ask your grown-up for the total, then check together.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Draw a strip story and ask a grown-up to find the total.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the boxes are the same size and that the total adds up.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen a strip. Put 4 counters in each of 3 cups. Show them the strip of 3 boxes and tell them the total.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Show a grown-up 3 cups of 4 counters and draw the strip.
menu.answer: 3 boxes with 4 in each box: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 counters.

parent.summary: We drew stories as strips: one box for each group, the same number in every box. We found the total, then did one more step (2 loose pens, or 2 marbles lost). We met twice as many: two equal strips, not 2 more. Equal-group stories are Primary 1 work. Strips and twice as many go a little beyond Primary 1 on purpose; we start from cups of counters.
words: strip: a row of equal boxes (a bar model at school)
each: how many are in one box or bag
loose: not in a box or a bag
twice as many: two equal strips
x: 'groups of', so 4 x 5 means 4 groups of 5
try_home: Cups: put 4 counters in each of 3 cups and draw 3 boxes with 4 in each. How many in all? Small things away from mouths.
Add a step: put 2 loose counters down, or take 2 away. What is the total now?
Twice as many: make a strip of 6, then twice as many. Is that 2 more?
ask: How many boxes? What is in each box?
What is step one? What is step two?
parent.when_stuck: Please do not teach a rule ('twice means times 2') or letters for unknowns: strips and counters are enough. Let your child use cups and counters, or draw boxes in a row, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking ‘how many boxes?’ and ‘what is in each box?’ works better than giving the answer. If the look-back page says ‘I am still stuck’, photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept 90 days after the program ends.

A grown-up cuts the strips page into ten strips of ten cells and cuts three of them after 6 cells (three strips of 6) BEFORE the lesson; nobody cuts during the lesson. Find 3 paper cups or plates and about 20 small things that are not food.
Have the slides open and have two or three paper strips and counters to show on camera if you wish. Check the strips are visible on screen share.

Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children's video is excluded; any voice that is not muted is recorded. Greet the whole group warmly, say the recording notice, then start the recording, and do not use children's first names while it runs.

Say plainly to families that equal-group stories are Primary 1 work, and that drawing strips (called bar models at school) and twice as many go a little beyond Primary 1 on purpose. Say strip to children. Twice as many is two equal strips, never "2 more". Do not call the lesson MOE-aligned. Term 2 lessons 5 to 8 build on one another.

Convention for twice as many and the key: either multiplication order is accepted (4 groups of 3 or 3 groups of 4 both give 12); ask 'how many boxes?' rather than marking it wrong. For T4, show the gap as two equal parts (6 and 6) before the word half.

workbook.hint_p1: Use cups and counters, or draw the strip. Every box is the same size.
workbook.hint_p2: Draw the strip if it helps. Do one step at a time.
workbook.hint_p3: Use strips or counters. Choose any question, in any order.
workbook.hint_p4: Choose any question. You do not have to finish them all.
workbook.home_hint: Use cups and counters or draw the strip. Small things stay on the table, away from mouths and little brothers and sisters.
